I have an interesting observation from the programmers on my team.

The good ones are increasingly producing good solutions much faster than before.

The not so good ones, are doing the same bullshit they did before, but now the don't even bother to check it. For example one requirement to "not implement it in the frontend" led to 3 times PR rejected, because it still has been implemented (even if it's partially there) in the frontend.

I'm not sure what's the reason, but I assume it's

- inability to understand architecture choices and their consequences

- "don't bother me with shit, just pay me a salary" attitude

but the AI lead to amplification of the good and the bad in people.

>"don't bother me with shit, just pay me a salary"

Well I'll admit this is me. Albeit previously I would have to generate working solutions meticulously to get my code reviewed and merged, as is normal. And it would be good work I could be proud of because _I_ wrote it!

But now the same people who would scrutinize me also outpace me with agents (the good developers you refer to) and also continue to scrutinize me. I recognize my own mediocrity in the face of my peers. So I don't know, I don't really care about my work quality anymore, the incentive of "do enough to put bread on the table" is now a much higher bar that I am struggling to meet.

This year has made me realize salary work really isn't a proper incentive to fully apply myself because being stuck under these guardrails and leadership decisions are a huge turn off. More than ever.

When you put a person who cares inside of a culture that doesn't and just wants to get things out to meet short term goals and figure out the cost later, you get this. Working on some projects its reasonable, but on others, especially services that customers really depend on where the cost of failure is high, it really is short term thinking. If speed is the only moat a company has, its just going to be death marches.

This situation sounds very similar to mine.

I'm also like: why would you give the execs more productivity for no additional pay? The puritanical love of work and individualistic competitiveness in the US is so counterproductive to any sort of gains in livelihood for the average person.

I'm not too familiar with the US workplace, but don't you have salary negotiations? Wouldn't you want more leverage for arguing for a higher salary, if you're unhappy with your salary? I'm also curious what work structure makes you feel like you're working for execs, rather than for your clients/customers/end-users. Surely you want the people who use your systems to have a smooth experience?

Making end users happy is a side effect. My own well being comes first.

You postulated this in another reply to me so I'll say here, why would I seek to make end users happy and work myself to the bone when leadership reaps the awards?

Even with salary negotiation there is almost no commensurate compensation you get under any employer that matches the value you bring to the company. That's how it's designed of course, by taking a base wage you trade off the risk of your income stream suddenly failing.

I am at that point now where that risk does not seem so scary anymore, which is odd to me. I never thought I'd consider taking the risk before. And I am learning that founders are usually driven by the feeling that I have.

Not really. American Corporations have successfully changed the culture to a point where asking about salary is considered a flaw to the worker. It somehow demonstrates a lack of loyalty.

Things are getting better, but HR still routinely preaches that you should never share your salary with anyone else. A lot of times they infer you will be fired for it.

Salary negotiations are sort of constrained to cost of annual living increases, or promotions. outside of that, you are not expected to ever talk about salary. ever.
I somewhat agree, but one is lucky to have any work at all these days, which unfortunately takes precedence.

This is the "got mine, fuck you" attitude that is part of the reason of a political shift to the right. And the worst part is, I get it, it's just also at odds with my more social leaning values.

Like, I don't mind paying taxes and social contributions, but I'm at a point now where I have to dip into my savings on the regular to match the monthly expenses and there hasn't been anything going in there for years.

I try to discern between the GMFY crowd and people who are just burnt out or dealing with life, because I have sympathy for the latter. Thankfully, the GMFY's will often be vocal with their dirtbaggery and let you know exactly who they are. They seem blissfully unaware that everyone is watching them and they are trashing their reputations.

I think the swing to the right is due to nation-state propaganda organs being defunded or replaced worldwide. People are naturally change averse, so either conservative or reactionary. Without the constant 'nudges', you're getting to see people's prickly natures coming out more.

> The puritanical love of work and individualistic competitiveness in the US is so counterproductive to any sort of gains in livelihood for the average person

History shows that it isn’t.
I'm always curious why people who don't care about work or tech spend time commenting on career sites and topics
Because they used to care.

Just because I am not happy with my employment situation doesn't mean I don't care about tech. I am privileged to even say that my job hasn't sucked all the joy out of building projects outside of work. None of this is a prerequisite for me ranting :)

Do you care about your users? If you care about tech, I'm sure you're as dissatisfied with the current state of broken and invasive software as the rest of us. I don't know the exact nature of your work, but don't you care about the experience of your clients or end-users?

Would you take a bullet for your clients and end-users?

Burning yourself out to patch over unsustainable working conditions is a slow bullet.

100%. I've been combating burnout over the last year or so. A saying that has stuck with me recently is "you don't need to set yourself on fire to make others warm." Trying to fix things by yourself in a massive bureaucracy is nigh impossible, so I've resigned myself to stop going the extra mile for the sake of the health and wellbeing of myself and my family.

Many smart people get bored and get all the joy sucked out of them when living and working under circumstances.

Some people enjoy the challenge and may compensate outside work hours, often doing overtime without compensation, that often implies less of a life outside of work or work concerns, promoting their personal branding, conferences, etc.

Just because these people exist and get rewarded does not mean their work environment is not predatory.
I like tech
Thank you for this honest take.
Thank you for posting. I felt almost like I was reading my own thoughts. You're not alone

You're lucky. Every single person (n of around 10) I've been unlucky enough to review code for lost between 0.5 and 3 promotion levels of competence when they started using LLM code generation, and it's been worse for the better programmers because they have more capacity to lose skills.

My personal "favorite" was when the lead engineer who onboarded me half a decade prior forgot the written policy he'd put in place of "no raw js dates. use this library for everything date related instead" and sent up an MR that not only used javascript dates, but did complex operations on them (incorrectly at that, because it didn't account for timezones, daylight saving, years that had a leap day, and months that weren't 30 days).

From what I can tell, it's the exact same reason people drive faster than is prudent or use their cellphone while driving. It feels safe and good right up until it isn't and you crash. And because most places don't have anywhere close to adequate specification detail, test coverage, or review coverage, the broken bits aren't even noticed until much later.

I think for a lot of people it's that they stopped caring or obsessing over the (perceived) small details; AI makes it very easy to work on a higher level. I suspect (don't quote me on this) that it's the same for a lot of developers that grew to more lead / managerial positions - at some point the details don't matter much to you personally and you need to spend your energy elsewhere.

But I hope people are gathering metrics. We had an extra meeting the other day because we're seeing an upwards trend in outages, the meeting was mainly about how it affects various departments (like customer support) and potential revenue loss (can't sell a product/service if the signup page is down for three days).

Thing is, there's no one cause for any of those - we have hundreds of engineers, dozens of applications and 3rd party integrations, millions of (potential) customers each running their own set of devices, and it's pretty much impossible to control everything.

But this goes beyond whether or not code was written by an attentive hand working under a strict set of policies or an AI that figures it out on the go, and goes up a level to things like realtime monitoring and incident responses.

You're right that as a person moves into management/staff+ that individual details matter less for them, because they begin to deal at a more strategic or operational level, but someone still needs to obsess over the small details (to make things easier, let's assume we're only talking about the details that actually matter and that there's broad agreement what that set is). It's not that those details stop mattering to them, it's that they have to depend on the assumption/promise that someone else is going to mind those details for them, so that they can work on things with a broader perspective.

The problem comes when no one is actually minding those details anymore. If those details aren't actually minded, then the work at the higher levels will be much less useful and effective, and in the worst cases won't matter at all.

I am seeing the same. The skillsets degrading rather rapidly, people not able to maintain focus and becoming less sharp in general. The brain rot associated with short form videos is affecting our industry via LLMs. It doesn't give me any joy to see it happening, especially to people I care about.

I don't know why I haven't been able to see the similarity between short form content and LLMs in our industry until reading your comment, but that is apt. That's the impression I'm getting. I stay away from "agentic code generation" as much as possible, just like I avoid short form content mills like the plague. That said, LLMs have been a huge boon for me as a research assistant. Being able to look up very niche problems, and have responses be tailored to me, is awesome. My brain stays sharp and I still enjoy the fun of putting the pieces together myself much faster than before.

I don't personally like LLMs for research assistance (yet?) because i can't get over the hallucinating or rather, waste too much time validating that it's not currently overcast when they tell me the sky is in fact blue.

But, especially as code gets flung over the wall faster and with less care, I do think they are getting to be pretty great at reviewing code for specific things that a linter can't easily catch and for looking for security, implementation, and architectural flaws before I have to look for them. A couple examples of what i mean: 'does the code use knex.raw with a template literal?', 'does the code do n+1 db lookups instead of something better?' 'do all the added/modified tests follow the test case template defined here?'
Agreed. I trust it more as a codebase query system rather than a codebase writer.
Amplifier of human intent. Do you want to work hard and cure cancer? Great! AI can help. Do you want to phone it in and do the bare minimum? AI can help you do that, too.

Long time ago, me and a friend of mine had a joke about PMs: to calculate how managers combine, you multiply their performance rates: two poor managers (e.g. 0.5*0.7) will give you worse performance than if you had one bad manager.
My similar formula about AI and developers is that it works like raising to the power of two: if you have a bad dev, you get 0.5^2: more mess more quickly. If you have a great dev, you get 1.5^2 - exponentially better :)
I've used an even less-kind framing in the past: incompetence is multiplicative. Two half-wits together gets you a quarter-wit.
I had a similar thought earlier this year - competence is additive, incompetence is multiplicative.
... quadratically better

Yes, these are my colleagues. Same crap as before. At least now I can setup an automatic ai review that is told what is not allowed (the errors they do all the time and refuse to learn) and I get PRs that have passed 8 review turns and are somewhat better.

I don’t think the good programmer bad programmer framing is helpful. I think AI fits the working style of some developers better than others. Where it fits I’ve seen some developers become so productive that they suck all the air out of the room and drown everyone else in review - not clear if this is good or bad. Where it doesn’t fit I’ve seen developers shut down because they find the workflow so depressing and their former productivity craters. Similarly I’ve seen perfectly good developers turn into slop generation machines and go largely unchecked because everyone else gets alarm fatigue from reviewing their PRs.

Yeah the review fatigue thing is a huge problem at the moment. When your work becomes 90% reviewing AI code, it is very demotivating.

I have been focusing a lot more on testing and "manual" validation than on reviewing individual lines of code. (And on setting up rules for what the lines of code should look like that are easily checked with deterministic tools or by llms.)

For large diffs, I’ll have the human driver walk me through the code in a call and if they understand it well enough to explain it to me, and explain the implications of the changes, that’s good enough for me; if they can’t answer how something works, I’ll respectfully turn down their contribution.

This cost shifting is how I stay sane and avoid burn out at work as well as stay apprised of major behavioral changes in the software we run.

I also think it’s important to emphasize that in an organization, individual productivity is secondary to group productivity, and group productivity is different than the sum of its parts.

I understand your reasoning but my reaction to this suggestion is very strong revulsion :) On both sides of it, I would despise this process.

But you're right about thinking in terms of group productivity and costs and incentives.

We solved this at work by creating a system that has an LLM read a Jira ticket assigned to Mike, create an implementation by itself and post a PR using a service account. Then Mike can come along and review it, thereby satisfying peer review as it was authored by a different user (in our SCM) than the one that reviewed it.

"don't even bother to check it."

I have to admit it gets really exhausting to review the AI output. It comes in so fast and more and more it's quite good. So it's very tempting to get more relaxed about reviews. I guess in a sense manual coding gave you some mental downtime while writing code. With AI you don't get that anymore. It's always full speed.

The problem is that humans are badly suited to remaining attentive in these circumstances. Take the combination of “overwhelming amount of output”, “99% of the time it does the right thing in the right way” and we are basically wired for vigilance to flag.
It makes me admire people like Linus Thorvalds. His job is mostly to read code and stay on top of the contributions of many people. I don’t think I could do that.
It’s easier to remain vigilant when a large part of the contributions are bad or incorrect than when it’s a very small percentage.

The PR reviewers delegate work to programmers, the programmers delegate the work to AI; then, the programmer reviews the AIs work, and the PR reviewer reviews the PR.

Those "architects" or other idea people should be reviewing the PRs and keeping an eye on the whole system. That's their job, right?

Usually the programmers are responsible for their own work, and then also reviewing their own work, which is just weird. The context switching is very draining.

The problem is that PR reviews are viewed as a side-task, and it's a thankless job. The guy who implemented the fancy new feature will be personally thanked by the CEO and taken out to lunch, the PR reviewer who pointed out in the original PR that it would corrupt the database gets a "nice catch" comment, and that's it.

This is one of those cases where companies unfortunately misalign their interests with yours.

Also, "confidence w/o ability" is the core of the Dunning-Kruger effect. You have to know a fair amount to understand how shit you are at things.

> Some not so good ones have even stopped using AI at all, arguing it 'just got confused'. Good ones on the other hand are embracing it

The behaviour of the good programmers is in my experience very "spread": some embrace strongly embrace LLMs for programming, some strongly reject LLMs for programming, with everything in-between.

The explanatory variables that I rather think are good predictors whether a good programmer will embrace or reject LLMs for coding are rather the following ones:

1. Is the programmer biased towards the "artisan" side of programming, or does he see the code as a means to an end?

2. Is the programmer either

- in love,

- interested in, or

- does the programmer have to work with

more obscure programming languages and/or the abstractions and mental models that these programming languages are based on? If this is the case, using an AI is often more of a hindrance than help because there exists much less training data, and/or the programmer will much more often be confronted with the observation that the AI model simply does not "get" what he wants, and will very often get annoyed by bad AI code hallucinations.

The best one I've seen aren't so interested in the "artisanal" part of the programming, but on the "practical engineering" part.

They constantly are poking at the requirements to understand what's the purpose and they find a better, simpler or sometimes hackier (for temporary stuff) solution, but they are on time, they solutions work and they get shit done.

I've seen some really crafty "artisanal" ones that debate for hours and rewrite 10 time the release scripts... Not the most efficient way to spend their time.

> "Adding agents to a project with unclear requirements gets you the wrong answer faster."

The thing is it gets you the wrong answer so fast it’s now the best way to figure out the right requirements.

Not if you turn off your brain. Never actually stop to question the path you're going down, because the speed is making you blind. Which is what I feel I see more and more. Or how do you even know it's the wrong answer if you didn't think it through before starting?

One example: setting the agent ablaze on some task, keeping it going, and after a few days of working with the agent you have a feature. But it's not what you were supposed to make. The agent didn't have all the context and made something slightly off, and you never internalized the problem enough to even spot it. If you actually stopped to think a bit on how the feature would have to work to tie it in with everything else, like you would have done before, you would've spotted it.

A simple observation here is that historically inter people communication is the main scaling bottleneck in software teams. It's what's behind the main premise in the mythical man month that adding more people to a team makes it slower. You increase the man months, but you are adding so much overhead that it's a net loss.

It's why big software companies struggle getting big things done whereas small and nimble startups tend to run circles around those. Google, Apple, Amazon, and Microsoft are great examples of companies that are really struggling with doing anything outside of the stuff they are already know how to do despite adding people by the thousands/tens of thousands. The more people they have the less likely any of them is going to be to do something completely new and different.

How does AI impact all this? It makes the problem (inter people communication) much worse. Imagine five people doing things manually. They have to sync up regularly. But there's only so much they can do in a day so they can stay in sync relatively easy. Scale that to 50. Now your meeting overhead becomes very non trivial.

Now add AI to the mix. Each of these people goes off and maxes out their tokens every day. They are refactoring, adding new sub systems/products, new UIs, etc. How do they coordinate their actions? How are they going to communicate their intentions and actions to each other. How do they brief each other on what's already been done?

The day to day scope of the massive amount of changes done by each of those individuals quickly grows way beyond whatever fits in typical/reasonable meeting structures. So, all the obvious things start happening: people either don't communicate or communicate poorly. They work against each other, break each other's work, etc. Everybody has a hard time staying on whatever is happening. The easy implication is exactly what we see happening in most big organizations: not much happening at all. They were already bottle necked on their size. AI made the problem much worse and as a result they aren't getting more done. At best they are maybe getting about the same stuff done with a bit less people.

AI clearly favors setups where you can minimize all of the communication. Small 1-3 person teams are probably a lot more optimal here. They always were and e.g. Jeff Bezos figured that out early in the life of Amazon (the two pizza rule). But AI just makes it much more obvious. Remove the need to sync lots of people and you free up time to actually do stuff (with or without AI).

The same dynamic probably holds to some extent with using multiple agents. If you are burning a lot of tokens and time on getting agents to sync with each other, that overhead is only going to get worse if you add more agents probably. And if you need to be in the loop to micro manage them, you become the bottleneck. Even if you just work by yourself. The trick is providing enough autonomy so you don't have to micro manage as much. And structuring your agents to minimize the amount of other agents each agent has to sync up with. The two pizza rule still holds.
